les: Wat mense oor die Maan vertel
kaps_punt: Maan stories - kulturele stories oor die Maan vertel ons oor die belangrikheid van die Maan in mense se lewens

items.bewering: Oral op aarde kyk mense na die Maan en vertel stories daaroor. Sulke stories wys hoeveel die Maan vir mense oor die hele wêreld beteken.
items.bron: Wikipedia, 'Lunar deity' (Moon figures and stories in Greek, Roman, Chinese, Aztec, Inca, Hindu, Japanese and other traditions); the four African traditions in this lesson, confirmed below, add to it. A general claim and it holds.

items.bewering: By die Zoeloe-mense word vertel van 'n hiëna wat 'n been in haar bek dra. Sy kom by die water en sien die Maan se beeld daarin. [...] Sy gooi self die been neer om die vleis in die water te vat.
items.bron: The core only: G. H. McKnight, 'The Middle English Vox and Wolf', PMLA 23(3), 1908, pp. 497-509 (quoted in Wikipedia, 'The Moon is made of green cheese'), mentions 'the Zulu tale of the hyena that drops the bone to go after the moon reflection in the water', alongside tales of Aarne-Thompson type 34. That is a single one-line scholarly mention. No primary Zulu text or full published retelling was found (searched in English, Afrikaans and isiZulu; Callaway and Bryant not reachable). So the attribution of the core motif rests on thin evidence, and the details are dealt with in the next two items.

items.bewering: Sy dink dit is 'n groot stuk vet vleis wat daar onder lê. [...] Sy hap met haar bek na die Maan in die water. Maar sy kry net water in haar bek en niks anders nie.
items.bron: Not found in any source. McKnight's mention does not say what the hyena took the reflection for (fat or meat) or how the episode played out. A different, unattributed hyena tale (C. H. Stigand, 'The Hyaena and the Moonbeam', in Black Tales for White Children) has the hyena take the reflection for a BONE and drink until it bursts, so even the published versions of this motif do not agree on the details. The lesson can only be checked against a published Zulu retelling, and none was found.

items.bewering: Toe kom 'n ander hiëna by die water en vat haar been.
items.bron: Not found in any Zulu source. This ending, where someone else gets the bone that was dropped, is not part of McKnight's mention. It looks like the ending of Aesop's dog and its reflection, or a writer's addition, rather than something taken from Zulu tradition. Unless a published Zulu version carries it, this is the riskiest sentence in the lesson, because it is the one most likely to be told as Zulu when it is not.

items.bewering: By die Khoikhoi of Nama word vertel dat die Maan 'n boodskap stuur: “Soos ek sterf en weer terugkom, so sal julle ook terugkom.”
items.bron: W. H. I. Bleek, Reynard the Fox in South Africa; or, Hottentot Fables and Tales (1864), Project Gutenberg #73413, Fables 31-34 'The Origin of Death': Fable 31 (Krönlein's manuscript, a Rhenish missionary among the Nama): 'As I die, and dying live, so ye shall also die, and dying live'; Fable 32 (Knudsen, Gross-Namaqualand, 1848): 'Like as I die and rise to life again, so you also shall die and rise to life again'. Also the Digital Bleek & Lloyd, story 114 'Moon and Hare: the origin of death', which calls it the Hottentot myth of the origin of death. Attribution to Khoikhoi/Nama is correct; the wording is a fair paraphrase.

items.bewering: Die Maan stuur 'n klein insek daarmee weg, maar die haas vat dit by die insek. Die haas dra dit self na die mense en sê dit verkeerd: “Soos ek sterf en nie terugkom nie, so sal julle ook nie terugkom nie.” Daarom kom mense nie weer terug nie.
items.bron: Bleek 1864, Fable 31: the Moon sends 'an Insect'; the Hare overtakes it, takes the message and tells men 'As I die, and dying perish, in the same manner ye shall also die and come wholly to an end'. Fable 32 (Knudsen) has the hare's version as 'Like as I die and do not rise to life again, so you shall also die, and not rise to life again'. Note for the person: the lesson's story is a COMPOSITE of two versions printed by Bleek. The insect comes from Fable 31; in Fable 32 and in ǂkasin's 1873 Bleek notebook version, the Moon gives the message to the hare directly. Every element is published Khoikhoi/Nama material, and the composite creates no contradiction.

items.bewering: Die Maan slaan die haas se lip oop, en dit is vandag nog geskeur.
items.bron: Bleek 1864, Fable 32 (Namaqua, Knudsen): the Moon beats the Hare on the mouth with a stick and slits it; Fable 33 (Priestley): a hatchet cuts his upper lip, the origin of the 'Hare-lip'; Digital Bleek & Lloyd story 114 motifs: 'origin (of the harelip)'. Versions differ on how it was done: Fable 31 says the Moon struck the nose with a piece of wood and 'the Hare's nose is slit'; ǂkasin's version has the Moon burn the mouth with a heated stone. The lesson's 'slaan ... lip oop' matches Fable 32 and leaves out what the Moon struck with, which keeps clear of the disagreement.

items.bewering: Die ǀXam-San vertel van die Maan wat hoog deur die lug loop. Die Son dra 'n skerp mes en sny nag na nag stukke van hom af. Die Maan word kleiner en kleiner totdat net sy ruggraat oorbly.
items.bron: W. H. I. Bleek & L. C. Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), ch. II 'Sun and Moon', 'The Children are sent to throw the sleeping Sun into the sky' (sacred-texts mirror sbf06): 'the Sun pierces it, with the Sun's knife ... therefore, it decays away'; Bleek, A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (1875), quoted in Specimens: 'This process is repeated until almost the whole of the Moon is cut away, and only one little piece left'. Digital Bleek & Lloyd, ||kabbo, 'The Sun pierces the full Moon with his knife' (1871). In this tradition the Moon is a man, which matches the lesson's 'hom'. Attribution to the ǀXam is correct.

items.bewering: Toe smeek hy die Son om hom te los ter wille van sy kinders. Die Son laat die ruggraat staan en loop verder. Uit daardie een stukkie ruggraat groei die Maan weer stadig aan. Nag na nag word hy groter, en op die ou end is hy weer vol.
items.bron: Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), same story: 'O Sun! leave for the children the backbone!' ... 'Therefore, the Sun leaves the backbone for the children'; '... he goes to become another moon, which is whole'. Bleek 1875: 'which the Moon piteously implores the Sun to spare for his (the Moon's) children. From this little piece, the Moon gradually grows again until it becomes a full moon'. Matches the published source.

items.bewering: Hierdie storie kom nie uit Suid-Afrika nie. Dit kom van die Maasai-mense in die suide van Kenia en die noorde van Tanzanië.
items.bron: eHRAF World Cultures (Yale), Maasai summary: the Maasai region is 'divided between southern Kenya, where most of the Maasai live, and northern Tanzania'; World History Encyclopedia, 'Maasai People': 'mainly lives in the area spanning southern Kenya and northern Tanzania'. The story is published as Maasai by Naomi Kipury, Oral Literature of the Maasai (1983).

items.bewering: By hulle word vertel dat die Son en die Maan getroud was. Die twee het eendag met mekaar baklei en mekaar lelik seergemaak. Die Son was skaam oor sy wond en wou dit vir almal wegsteek. Hy het toe so fel begin skyn dat niemand na hom kan kyk nie. Die Maan was nie skaam oor haar wonde nie. Daarom kan jy haar wonde vandag nog van die aarde af sien.
items.bron: Naomi Kipury, Oral Literature of the Maasai (East African Educational Publishers, Nairobi, 1983), reproduced at bluegecko.org 'Maasai fables and legends - the Sun and the Moon': 'In the beginning the sun married the moon'; they fought and wounded each other (she wounds his forehead; he scratches her face and plucks out an eye); the sun is embarrassed and says 'I am going to shine so hard that people will not be able to look at me'; the moon feels no shame, and 'you will see the wounds that the sun inflicted on her'. Wikipedia 'Olapa' (citing Kipury) agrees: 'To hide his shame, he took to shining very brightly, so that no one could look straight at him.' Matches the published source.

items.bewering: ruggraat: Die ry klein beentjies wat in die middel van jou rug loop.
items.bron: Cleveland Clinic, 'Spine: Anatomy, Function, Parts' and NCBI StatPearls, 'Anatomy, Back, Vertebral Column': a column of 33 small bones (vertebrae) stacked down the back. Read on its own, the entry is true and complete enough for Grade 4. In the block it applies to the Moon's backbone, which is fine as a figure of speech in a story.

opsomming: The ǀXam, Khoikhoi/Nama and Maasai stories are attributed correctly and told as their published sources tell them (the Khoikhoi one combines two versions Bleek printed, without contradicting either), and the definition and the place facts are right; but for the Zulu hyena story, only a single 1908 scholarly mention of the core was found, and the details that the hyena thought it was fat meat and that another hyena took the bone were found in no source, so a person must decide whether to cut those details down to the attested core or find a published Zulu version; there are no superlatives or analogies in the lesson.
